titleText.es: ―No lo sé. ¿Por qué no se te cae la boina de la cabeza? ―Grapas.
titleText.en: —I don't know. Why doesn't your beret fall off your head? —Staples.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: they took; pulled (someone or something) out
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Sacaron is a completed-past form of sacar used for more than one doer. Sacar often means moving someone or something from inside to outside.

example.en: They took the boxes out of the car.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: by; with (as part of a empujones, “by shoving”)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In the fixed expression a empujones, a introduces the repeated pushes that describe how something moves. It is not the usual destination meaning of a.

example.en: They moved the table by shoving it.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; part of de cabeza (“headfirst”)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In the fixed movement expression de cabeza, de introduces the body part that leads. The two words work together rather than using de in its ordinary “of” sense.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: through; along; down; via (a movement path)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Por can mark the path followed during movement. English may choose through, along, down, or via according to the route.
Actúas comes from actuar. The ending -as identifies one person addressed informally, and the written accent keeps the stress on ú.
Digno describes a masculine singular person or thing. Use digna for a feminine singular person or thing.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something moves because it is shoved repeatedly?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a empujones to mean “by shoving” or “with repeated pushes.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Empujón means one push or shove. Spanish normally uses its plural, empujones, after a in this fixed expression. The complete expression describes the manner of movement; neither word changes.

example.en: They moved the table by shoving it.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that a person or thing moves with the head leading?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put de cabeza after the movement verb to mean “headfirst.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Cabeza means “head.” In this fixed expression, de does not have its ordinary “of” meaning; de cabeza describes the direction or manner of the movement. The expression stays unchanged.

example.en: He fell headfirst into the water.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: verbo en forma de ellos/ellas sin agente nombrado
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can Spanish describe an action by unnamed people, where English might use a vague “they” or a passive sentence?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the plural “they” form of the verb and do not name who performed the action.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plural verb ending points to people who did the action, but the speaker leaves them unidentified. Depending on the context, English may use “they,” “people,” “someone,” or a passive form such as “was built.” For a completed regular -ar action, the plural ending is -aron, as in llamaron.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you intensify a describing word to mean “so,” as in “so difficult”?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put tan immediately before the word that describes the person, thing, or action.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tan does not change form. It goes before an adjective, a word that describes a person or thing, or before an adverb, a word that describes an action. Use forms of tanto instead before a noun or when saying “so much” or “so many.”

regions.labelEs: TE SACARON A EMPUJONES DE CABEZA POR LA VAGINA DE ALGUIEN. ¿POR QUÉ ACTÚAS TAN DIGNO?

applications.explanationEn: Sacaron is a plural completed-past verb, while the people who performed the action are left unnamed.
A and the plural noun empujones form the fixed expression for movement caused by repeated shoves.
De cabeza describes the head as leading the movement.
The two written words por qué ask for a reason, and qué carries a written accent.
Tan immediately precedes digno and intensifies that description.
